commits.message:
Complexity guards: devEngines asks for the Node with threadCpuUsage, a self-test pins that time off the CPU is not counted, full-size output checks are back, and near-floor sizes are doubled (rich-unfiled-791c.xrxj)

Review (high) of #460: process.threadCpuUsage exists from Node 22.19 / 23.9,
which devEngines (^22.18.0 || >=23.6.0) did not require; the self-tests only
simulated load with CPU work both clocks count, so reverting to wall time stayed
green; the 3-element output checks dropped the at-scale correctness the
budget tests had; four smaller runs sat under 15 ms of CPU here, about 2x the
floor on a runner twice as fast.

Complexity guards assert how their time grows, on the thread's CPU time, instead of a wall-clock budget (rich-unfiled-791c.xrxj)

The ten remaining guards that timed one run against a 1 s or 2 s budget
now assert growth through expectLinearTime, one call per workload so a
quadratic one cannot hide behind a larger linear one beside it. Each was
run against the super-linear code it guards: the commit before its fix,
or, where that code only ever existed mid-PR, a reconstruction (the RUN
and TRAILING_RUN_RE lookbehinds dropped, a whole-list filter per plugin
pair, a quote re-read per lazy line). Every one read 13-229x for 4x.
JSONHighlighter was never quadratic on any of the runs but digits; its
cases stay as the contract the describe states.

expectLinearTime now reads process.threadCpuUsage, not performance.now.
Inside the full suite a linear highlighter's larger run took two to three
times as long as alone while its smaller one did not, reading 8.8-10.9x:
a run shorter than a scheduler slice escapes oversubscription that a
longer one pays for its whole length, so a wall-clock ratio does not
cancel load. Three full-suite runs green after the change.

The Markdown guards time parsing only. Drawing a long paragraph is
quadratic in Segment.divide, filed as rich-unfiled-791c.vzmy.

Markdown counts a tab after a nested quote's `>` from the content of the quote around it, as markdown-it does (rich-unfiled-791c.g10i) (#459)

* Markdown counts a tab after a nested quote's `>` from the content of the quote around it, as markdown-it does (rich-unfiled-791c.g10i)

markdown-it resets bsCount at each `>` to the column past it measured from
the enclosing quote's content, not cumulatively, so past the second `>` its
tab stops are not the source's. It also measures the whitespace after a `>`
in the enclosing quote's columns while cutting indentation in the new
quote's, so the two can disagree. A Line now carries both: `lead` (sCount)
and `text` re-based on the quote's content (bsCount), plus `written` so a
cut that stops before an item's marker keeps the marker, as getLines does.

A differential fuzz of 6000 nested-quote inputs against Rich 15 went from
1661 differing to 15, none newly wrong; the 15 are rich-unfiled-791c.jlk3.

* A Line holds its text once, as written, and how many leading characters are list markers, not a blanked copy beside it (rich-unfiled-791c.g10i)

text and written had to stay aligned character for character, and nothing
held them to it; a spread replacing one would have desynchronised
dropColumns. The markers now read as spaces wherever columns are counted.

* The blockquote comment says a quote reads its `>` lines from its content on, as quoted() now builds them (rich-unfiled-791c.g10i)
